newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analyst sees slow growth for aluminium use in cars.
newsitem.headline: Analyst sees slow growth for aluminium use in cars.

text.p: Aluminium should capture market share from steel in car body structures, but progress will be slow and vulnerable to competition from plastics, a metals analyst told a Metal Bulletin aluminium conference on Monday.
"...steel will clearly retain its position as the dominant body structure," said Paul Williams of London-based Commodity Research Unit (CRU).

Under current assumptions, the aluminium body sheet market over the next 20 years would not get anywhere near the size of the market for aluminium can stock, as was hoped in some parts of the industry, he said.
Can stock currently absorbs 3.4 million tonnes of aluminium a year while the use of aluminium in car structures and exterior panels represents just 30,000 tonnes per year.
Williams said aluminium extrusion demand from carmakers was promising, especially in Europe, with the uptake of spaceframe vehicle designs.
But mass volume designs needed to be introduced to secure aluminium use and electric cars, which would favour aluminium-structured designs, were only a minor market to date.
It could not be ruled out, though, that unforeseeable rises in petrol prices, for example, might boost the use of aluminium in cars.
Audi AG in 1994 introduced the luxury A8 vehicle using Alcoa's spaceframe construction technique and Hydro Aluminium is also active in promoting this form of manufacture.

An Audi representative at the conference, Karl-Heinz von Zengen of Audi's Neckarsulm works, said the A8 was a succesful luxury car but many obstacles needed to be overcome to move into mass production.

Formability and strength of aluminium alloys and of welding processes needed to be improved, thin-walled extrusions needed to be produced, and light, rigid and high-strength parts with high geometrical tolerance needed to be developed.

CRU's Williams also said that as carmakers were becoming more versatile, thermoplastics might be able to offer the desired qualities in new structural materials, making aluminium's future share transitory.
